title: JSON to YAML: Field and Type Boundaries When Converting
description: How JSON to YAML conversion works, and how the four directions handle field names, XML attributes, YAML anchors, and types, with boundaries and a checklist.
content:
Converting JSON to YAML is direct: open the JSON/XML/YAML Converter, choose JSON → YAML under Conversion Direction, paste a strictly valid JSON document, and click Convert to get YAML. The tool validates the input with JSON.parse first, then hands it to a YAML library for serialization. Invalid JSON fails immediately with an error; differences in types, key names, and line breaks are left for you to check.

Choosing the Direction: JSON to YAML in Practice

All four directions share the same input and output boxes; only the Conversion Direction dropdown differs. JSON → YAML takes the shortest path and exposes no extra options: indentation, quoting, and value formatting all follow the YAML library's defaults.

  1. Paste the JSON you want to convert into Input Source Data, and first make sure it is plain JSON with no comments or trailing commas brought along.
  2. Select JSON → YAML under Conversion Direction.
  3. Click Convert; the result appears in the output box on the right. On error the status bar shows a message and the output box is cleared.
  4. Take the YAML with Copy, paste it into the target file, and confirm that indentation and quotes survived intact.

The premise here is that the JSON itself is valid. JSON property names must be double-quoted, no trailing comma is allowed, and // or /* */ comments are not permitted; those forms may work in JavaScript object literals, but none of them is valid JSON. If the input is “JSON with comments” copied from a config file, find the syntax error with the JSON Formatter & Validator first, then come back and convert.

A minimal example follows. The tool's built-in sample is isomorphic to it; in this example the converted YAML keeps the writing order from the JSON, the string 3.0 gains quotes, and the array becomes a two-space-indented dash list.

{
  "name": "Clover",
  "version": "3.0",
  "free": true,
  "tags": ["dev", "tools"]
}
name: Clover
version: "3.0"
free: true
tags:
  - dev
  - tools

The output ends with one trailing newline and, by default, no --- document start marker. These details are not decoration: YAML's implicit typing rules read unquoted 3.0 as a number and true as a boolean; keeping a string a string depends on the quotes.

What Each of the Four Directions Does

Putting the four directions in one table makes the differences clear: the two XML directions have fixed key-name conventions, while the two YAML directions depend on the YAML library's parsing and serialization.

DirectionImplementation pathOutput characteristics
JSON → XMLGenerate elements recursively after JSON.parseThe root element is always root; object keys become tag names; array element names come from the key name with a trailing s removed
XML → JSONParse into a DOM with DOMParser, then read recursivelyAttributes get an @ prefix; a child element with the same name appears once as an object and multiple times as an array; leaf text goes into #text
JSON → YAMLCall the YAML library's stringify after JSON.parseTwo-space indentation, no document start marker; strings containing newlines are emitted as literal blocks
YAML → JSONThe YAML library's parse, then JSON.stringify(…, null, 2)JSON with two-space indentation; comments and anchor names are not preserved, a leading --- is dropped, and multi-document input errors out

Every entry in this table can be matched against the page script: the XML direction has no branch that generates attributes, so a field in JSON can never become an XML attribute; JSON → YAML passes no indentation or quoting options, and YAML → JSON only fixes JSON indentation at two spaces, so formatting on the YAML side follows the library's defaults.

Where Field Names and Hierarchy Get Lost

Start with key names. JSON → XML accepts only keys that begin with a letter or underscore and continue with letters, digits, underscores, dots, or hyphens; keys that do not match the rule are written uniformly as item. When two invalid keys appear together, the output contains two item elements, and reading it back into JSON merges them into an array; the original key names can no longer be recovered.

{"2fa": true, "first name": "Clover"}

This JSON produces two <item> elements rather than <2fa> and <first name>. Array naming has another easily overlooked quirk: the element name is the outer key with one trailing s removed, so tags becomes tag and items becomes item, but status becomes statu and address becomes addres. English fields whose names end in s get deformed in XML.

XML → JSON follows a different set of conventions. Attributes are written as @ plus the attribute name, and the text of a leaf element as #text; a child element with the same name appears as an object when there is only one and as an array when there are two or more. That creates an irreversible ambiguity: “an array with a single element” and “a single object” look identical in XML, and converting back to JSON can only degrade to an object.

Run {"id": 1} through JSON → XML → JSON and id becomes {"#text": "1"}, while the root node also gains #text: "1". The reason is that the tool's XML output is indented, so the root's first child node is a whitespace text node, and reading it splices that whole stretch of text into #text as well. The number 1 becomes a string, and the root element name is lost too: JSON → XML always emits <root>, and XML → JSON reads only the contents of the document element without keeping the outer tag name.

Attributes cannot come back either. A key such as @id does not satisfy the XML tag-name rules, so JSON → XML writes it as <item>; the attribute value survives, but the structural information that “this was an attribute” is gone. XML namespace prefixes, which contain a colon, run into the same problem.

Values and Line Breaks: Types the Text Layer Cannot Show

JSON has only six kinds of values: object, array, number, string, true/false, and null. XML does not carry scalar types the way JSON and YAML do; its content is all character data, so once a conversion passes through XML, type information is largely reduced to text.

1 and "1" in JSON both become <id>1</id> after JSON → XML, and xml2json reads both back as {"#text": "1"}; the boolean true becomes the string "true"; null, an empty object {}, and an empty array [] all emit self-closing elements and read back as an empty string. Three different values are flattened into one shape at the XML layer.

{"id": 1, "ok": true, "note": null}

YAML is different: it has implicit typing, and the parser recognizes unquoted scalars as booleans, integers, floats, or null according to the schema. YAML 1.2's core schema treats only true, True, TRUE and false, False, FALSE as booleans, so yes, on, and tRuE remain strings; 1.0 is read as the number 1, 0123 as decimal 123, 0x1F as 31, and ~ as null.

flag: yes
ratio: 1.0
code: 0123
hex: 0x1F
empty: ~

Converted to JSON, this is {"flag":"yes","ratio":1,"code":123,"hex":31,"empty":null}. To keep a leading zero such as 0123, you must quote it in YAML; conversely, when going JSON → YAML, the strings "true" and "123" are quoted by the serializer so they do not turn into a boolean or a number when read back. Delete those quotes by hand in the YAML output and the types flip.

Line breaks are another spot. A \n inside a JSON string usually becomes a literal block in JSON → YAML, and the block header varies with the content: |- when there is no trailing newline, | when there is one, |+ for multiple trailing newlines, and an indentation indicator such as |2- when leading spaces are present; YAML still reads it back as newlines. YAML multi-line text becomes an ordinary string containing \n after conversion to JSON. XML is coarser: reading trims textContent first, so leading and trailing whitespace is not preserved; with a single child element whose first child node holds text, no #text is added, and in the remaining cases with child elements the code writes the trimmed whole textContent (unless it is empty), while with more than one child element the inner indentation and newlines are kept in the concatenated text.

Boundaries and Limitations

Treat this tool as a “structure mover” rather than a “lossless converter”; confirm each of the following boundaries one by one.

  • XML attributes have no JSON counterpart. XML → JSON keeps attributes with the @ prefix, but JSON → XML does not recognize that convention, and @id is written as item. Attributes can only be inspected in the XML → JSON direction, and they are necessarily lost on the way back.
  • Comments and whitespace are not preserved. JSON does not support comments; YAML's # comments are discarded during parsing; XML comments are not character data and never enter the child element list or textContent. XML indentation is only layout, but whitespace text nodes take part in the firstChild/#text decision: when a single child element is preceded by whitespace, the root gains a trimmed #text. YAML indentation is syntax: change it and the parse result changes.
  • Mixed content loses text. When text and elements are interleaved (for example <root>a<b>1</b>c</root>), a single child element with a text first node leaves innerText empty, and the a and c text is lost.
  • Anchors, aliases, and multiple documents. YAML's &anchor and *alias point to the same object after parse, so JSON.stringify writes the content twice and the anchor name never appears; multiple documents separated by --- in one stream are not all read by a single parse — the tool calls parse only, so multi-document input reports Source contains multiple documents; duplicate keys with the same name also error.
  • Numbers and booleans are inferred only by YAML. YAML core schema rules decide true/false, integers, floats, and null; JSON's number syntax does not allow NaN or Infinity literals; XML is all text. Across the three formats, a type exists only at the layer whose parser recognizes it.
  • Key order is not a contract. The JSON specification defines an object as an unordered collection, and YAML defines a mapping as unordered as well; serializers usually emit in traversal order, but do not rely on that order for diffs or signatures.
  • Special characters are escaped, control characters are not. JSON → XML escapes the four characters &, <, >, and ", so they can go into text safely; but the character range XML 1.0 allows excludes most C0 control characters, so a JSON string carrying something like U+0001 produces XML that is not well-formed.
  • Round trips are not guaranteed to be lossless. Root element names, XML attributes, the shape of empty values, single-element arrays, comments, and anchors can all change; the tool's own description also states outright that round trips are not lossless, so do not mistake “conversion succeeded” for “semantically equivalent”.
  • Large files have no streaming. The page reads the whole text at once, and the XML direction also builds a complete DOM; input and output both stay in text boxes, so memory and responsiveness suffer with large files, and bulk data is better handled with command-line tools.

Checklist Before Delivery

  1. Confirm the JSON is valid with the JSON Formatter & Validator first, then start converting.
  2. For XML input, first use the XML Formatter to check that tags are closed and the hierarchy matches expectations.
  3. After YAML → JSON, spot-check critical paths with the JSONPath Tester to confirm no array was flattened into an object.
  4. Compare key names between source and target item by item, especially keys containing spaces, starting with a digit, or ending in s.
  5. Spot-check the five value kinds — null, empty object, empty array, number, and boolean — and confirm none became an empty string or a string.
  6. Parse the result once inside the target system for real, rather than judging by whether the text box looks right.

If the goal is only to turn a JSON config into YAML, the safest approach is to keep the structure simple: start key names with a letter, avoid a trailing s, keep arrays homogeneous, and quote strings when they need quoting. That way, even with the converter's naming and typing conventions, the result is easier to verify.

faqs.q: Why does JSON to YAML add quotes around strings automatically?
faqs.a: YAML infers the type of an unquoted scalar from the schema: 3.0 is read as a number and true as a boolean. The serializer quotes these strings so that they are still strings when read back; delete the quotes by hand and the type changes.

faqs.q: What are the extra @ and #text after XML to JSON?
faqs.a: The @ prefix means an XML attribute, and #text means the text inside an element. They are this tool's key-name conventions, not part of the JSON standard; when the result is converted back to XML, @ keys are not restored as attributes.

faqs.q: Why did an array with a single element turn into an object?
faqs.a: XML has no array type. When a child element with the same name appears once, xml2json emits an object; only two or more occurrences produce an array. XML itself cannot distinguish “a single-element array” from “a single object”, so that information is lost in conversion.

faqs.q: Why do yes and on not become booleans in YAML?
faqs.a: YAML 1.2's core schema parses only true, True, TRUE and false, False, FALSE as booleans; yes and on are ordinary strings. Write true or false when you need a boolean, and avoid relying on YAML 1.1 habits.

focus: Confirm the JSON is valid first, then decide how field names, empty values, and types should land in XML or YAML.
notice: Conversion runs locally in the browser and uploads no data; the tool does not guarantee lossless round trips — XML attributes, comments, and anchors may be lost on the way back.
